Schumer led Democrats to big Senate win. Now, some say they need a new leader

22 November, 2026 05:00 pm IST

By Nolan D. McCaskill WASHINGTON, Nov 22 (Reuters) – Chuck Schumer led Senate Democrats through November’s midterm elections that gave them a decisive 56-seat majority. Progressives responded with a collective “thank you, next,” arguing he should now make way for a successor.

Critics say Schumer’s decades in Washington, his age and his close ties to the party establishment make him ill-suited to lead a caucus increasingly shaped by younger, anti-establishment lawmakers.

“We write first to thank you,” leaders of the populist Working Families Party, which backs like-minded Democratic candidates in elections, said in a November 13 letter to Schumer that called for a generational leadership change.

Show Full Article

“If you step aside at the height of a victory you helped secure, you would show voters that the Democratic Party heeded their call for change. The new majority can begin its work united and focused on fighting for the people who elected them.”

The top Democrat in the Senate for the past decade, Schumer, who turns 76 on Monday, has projected confidence that his colleagues will choose to keep him as their leader in a secret vote on December 1.

“I will be elected majority leader,” Schumer, who is strongly favored to win, told reporters matter-of-factly last week.

But in the first contested Senate Democratic leadership race since 1994, the New York senator faces a challenge from Senator Chris Van Hollen, 67. While only modestly younger than Schumer, the Maryland lawmaker and his progressive allies outside the Capitol have cast him as an agent of change.

Van Hollen has said the 2026 results show voters are demanding the party break with the status quo and adopt a bolder approach that gives new voices, including incoming progressive lawmakers, more influence in the caucus.

‘TIME FOR NEW IDEAS’

The Maryland Democrat has run an increasingly public campaign, though the outcome will be determined in private by 56 Senate Democrats. At least 16 Democrats have publicly committed to backing Schumer, while only six have said they will vote for Van Hollen.

“I’m in this to win it,” Van Hollen said on Thursday. “That’s my goal. I think if we want to move forward on an ambitious agenda like this, we need new leadership. We need to change the culture of the Democratic caucus. People need to have more input. Our new members need to be at the table.”

Democrats flipped nine Senate seats in November, including in several states President Donald Trump won by double digits in 2024. Many of the incoming freshmen said during their campaigns that they would oppose Schumer for Democratic leader.

“Do I like Chuck Schumer?” asked Senator-elect Troy Jackson of Maine. “He’s been great, but I do think it’s time for new ideas.”

In an interview last week on CNN’s “State of the Union,” Van Hollen cited a “hunger for change” among Senate Democrats and said two incoming senators won despite Schumer’s efforts to back their primary opponents. He criticized Schumer for aligning with powerful pro-Israel and cryptocurrency interests in those races.

PROGRESSIVES BACK VAN HOLLEN

Senator-elect Abdul El-Sayed of Michigan said Van Hollen stands out because he understands how Washington and the Senate work as a past chair of House and Senate Democrats’ respective campaign arms, and he’s willing to take risks.

“Those two things are what we need right now, and we need to rethink the way we legislate,” he said, pointing to Van Hollen’s trips to advocate for a wrongly deported migrant and to draw attention to Israel’s war in Gaza as examples of his willingness to take risks.

Senator Tim Kaine of Virginia suggested the leadership fight reflected a healthy discussion within the caucus about its future direction. “And there’s nothing wrong with that,” he told Reuters.

Senate Democratic leader is the only unresolved role among Congress’ top four positions. House Democrats last week nominated Hakeem Jeffries to be speaker in the next Congress, where John Thune will continue to lead Senate Republicans and Representative Jim Jordan will succeed Speaker Mike Johnson as the top House Republican.

SCHUMER COULD FACE PRIMARY CHALLENGER IN 2028

Schumer is up for reelection in 2028, and losing the leadership race could make him a more vulnerable target, as ambitious Democrats such as Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez consider running for his seat. A memo from Ocasio-Cortez’s campaign acknowledged she could run for president, Senate or reelection to the House in 2028.

For his part, Schumer has swatted down questions about his future beyond the leadership election.

“I’m focused on 2027 and delivering for the American people,” he said on Wednesday.

(Reporting by Nolan D. McCaskill; Editing by Michael Learmonth and Cynthia Osterman)

By Sarah McFarlane and Peter Hobson ANTALYA, Turkey, Nov 22 (Reuters) – Two days after the official close of UN climate talks, COP31 presidents Australia and Turkey struggled to win consensus for a deal to advance the fight against climate change, raising the prospect of no deal being reached.

A new draft deal released on Sunday has yet to be approved as countries disagreed over issues including whether the accord should mention the fossil fuels scientists say are driving warming.

“While no one obtained everything they might have desired, everyone can find a place for themselves within this text. That is the very essence of consensus,” COP31 President Murat Kurum told the talks. “I hope that the decision emerging from this hall will demonstrate to the world that multilateralism is still capable of yielding results.”

Show Full Article

If approved, the current deal would acknowledge for the first time that global warming is on course to exceed the 1.5-degree Celsius (2.7-degree Fahrenheit) threshold that countries had sought to preserve, while calling for faster development of carbon-removal technologies to eventually reverse the overshoot.

Ireland’s environment minister Darragh O’Brien said the European Union could not support the proposed deal.

“We will not endorse a decision that does not respond to the science, that disregards the implementation gap, and that actually risks deepening the chasm between global commitments and the action required to correct the overshoot and bring 1.5 degrees back to within reach,” he said.

Panama also said it could not support the current text.

DRAFT OMITS MENTION OF FOSSIL FUELS

The current draft omits mention of fossil fuels and instead includes language referring to a previous COP at which governments agreed to transition away from oil, gas, and coal.

Observers at the venue, where catering outlets and exhibits have already been dismantled, said Saudi Arabia and other big oil-producing nations had pushed hard in negotiations for keeping explicit mention of fossil fuels out of the text, and carbon removal in.

“It seems like we are negotiating with the Saudis,” said Tuvalu’s climate minister, Maina Talia.

A representative for the Saudi delegation declined to comment.

Speaking on condition of anonymity, several delegations raised the prospect of leaving without a deal.

Others said they worried that too many delegations had already left to catch their planes home, making it possible there would not be a quorum for a decision.

“We hope, of course, that we will still reach a decision. But given the last few hours, I’m sceptical that this can still succeed in the short time left, especially since many colleagues have already left,” said Carsten Schneider, Germany’s environment minister.

Jennifer Morgan, former German climate envoy and a senior fellow at The Fletcher School at Tufts University, said: “After the presidency ignored the views of 150 countries and tabled a very weak text, negotiations are on the brink.”

FOSSIL FUELS STICKING POINT

Environmental group 350.org said it was disappointed by the draft’s failure to mention fossil fuels explicitly, as well as its encouragement of carbon-removal technologies.

“Carbon capture is one of the biggest scams of the overshoot era, and our leaders are on the verge of falling for it,” said Sara Shaw, the group’s campaigns and networks director, referring to the practice of trapping carbon dioxide before it reaches the atmosphere.

Critics say the technologies are expensive and unproven at scale, and that including them in a deal is likely to spur continued oil and gas development.

The new draft text followed intensive consultations between Australia, which is leading the talks, Turkey, which is hosting the meeting, and delegations from nearly 200 countries.

The presidency gave delegations several hours to raise any objections to the deal, with a session scheduled later on Sunday to begin approving it.

Australia’s task, supported by Turkey, has been to find a deal that balances the needs of nations most vulnerable to climate change with those whose economies depend on either the production or consumption of fossil fuels.

This year’s COP is the first since the UN’s environmental body confirmed that the rise in global temperature was set to exceed 1.5C, a threshold all countries agreed over a decade ago to try not to exceed, and beyond which extreme weather impacts intensify.

(Reporting by Ali Kucukgocmen, Tuvan Gumrukcu, Ezgi Erkoyun, Sarah McFarlane, Valerie Volcovici, Lewis Jackson, Simon Jessop and Peter Hobson; Writing by William James and Richard Valdmanis; Editing by William Mallard and Barbara Lewis)
